<document>
# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
This follow-up directly answers the question every earlier document left open: whether the per-hour gain persists. On the evidence presented, the answer is largely convincing. A gain remains at 24 months under a randomised design with record-based output, smaller than at nine months but clearly above zero. The arithmetic reproduces. The main problems are a misleading comparison in the Summary, an undefined hours measure, and a mediation result presented as more confirmatory than it is.

## 1. Arithmetic check

| Figure | Calculation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Output per hour, timesheets, 24 months | 0.966 / 0.88 | +9.8% ✓ |
| Output per hour, logs, 24 months | 0.966 / 0.89 | +8.5% ✓ |
| Decline on timesheets, 9 to 24 months | 9.8 / 12.5 | −22% ("about a quarter") ✓ |
| Meetings, treated relative to control | (3.9 − 7.4) − (7.0 − 7.2) | −3.3 hours ✓ |
| Mediation shares | 47 + 18 + 35 | 100% ✓ |
| Halden continuers, hours | 34.9 / 40.3 | −13.4% ✓ |
| Halden continuers, per hour | 96.8 / 86.6 | +11.8% ✓ |
| Counter staffing needed | 1 / 0.886 | about 13% more output per employee needed, so about 12% more staff ✓ |

One small coincidence to check: the 11 Halden continuers have a baseline of exactly 40.3 hours, the same figure as the 27 time-tracking organisations in the re-analysis. They are different subsets, so this may be chance, but it is worth confirming.

## 2. Main issues

**The Summary compares two different hours measures.**
- "Fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months" sets the nine-month timesheet estimate against the 24-month log estimate.
- The like-for-like timesheet comparison, which the body uses correctly, is 12.5% to 9.8%.
- So the Summary overstates the decline: about a third instead of about a fifth.
- Report the timesheet trajectory as the trend, and the log estimate separately as a robustness check on the hours measure.

**"Active log-in time" needs to be defined, and may not be the "stricter" measure.**
- If it records time spent working in the case-management system, it is not a superset of timesheet hours. It excludes meetings, email and phone work, and still misses unrecorded off-system work such as email at home, which was the original concern.
- In that case, output per log-hour measures how fast staff work on cases, which is a different quantity from output per hour worked.
- It would then also be odd as the outcome for a meetings mediator, since meeting time falls outside the denominator.
- If instead it means total logged-in session time, say so.
- The table shows no nine-month log figure, yet the 24-month value is a difference-in-differences that requires pre-period logs. If pre-period logs could be extracted retrospectively, report the nine-month value too.

**The mediation test is not an independent confirmation.**
- The hypothesis was generated on the same seven treated offices, the registration came at month 11 after the nine-month results were known, and the data overlap the period in which the pattern was first seen.
- Registration prevents analytic flexibility, which is valuable. But this is a pre-specified re-test on the same units, not a replication.
- "A larger sample of office-months" overstates the information. With 7 v 7 clusters, the effective sample is 14. An interval of 28% to 66% looks narrow for that; please state how clustering was handled and whether a small-sample correction was applied.
- The limitations rightly note that mediator–outcome confounding is possible. For example, better-managed offices may both cut meetings and work faster.
- The re-analysis was right that the original finding was exploratory. It was wrong to dismiss it outright. The fair conclusion is that the hypothesis held up on registered re-test, and now needs testing in new offices.

**A simple accounting check suggests meetings may explain more than 47%.**
- On timesheets, treated staff's hours fell by about 4.5 a week (12% of about 37.9). Meeting time fell by 3.5 hours. So time outside meetings fell by only about 1 hour, roughly 3%.
- Relative to control (whose time outside meetings rose slightly), that is about a 4% fall, against an output change of −3.4%.
- So output per hour outside meetings is roughly unchanged. If meetings produce little direct output, reallocating time away from them could account for nearly all of the per-hour gain, not 47%.
- The two approaches answer different questions, so they need not agree. But reconciling them would sharpen the interpretation, and the accounting version is easier for readers to grasp.

**The baseline meeting data need a source.** The nine-month report said calendar data were collected only in month six. Table 2's baseline figures (7.4 and 7.2 hours) must therefore have been reconstructed afterwards. Say how, as this is the pre-period figure the confirmatory claim rests on.

**The marketing agency doesn't fit "client-facing or coverage obligations."**
- An agency reverting because of client deadlines is a discretionary-work setting struggling, not a coverage problem.
- Folding it into the coverage category blurs the distinction the authors themselves introduced.
- It is a useful case on its own: deadline-driven discretionary work can also be strained by shorter hours.

## 3. Secondary points

- **The decline isn't statistically established.** The nine-month (+6.9 to +18.4) and 24-month (+4.6 to +15.2) intervals overlap heavily.
  - "Consistent with some fading" in the body is right. "Declined by about a quarter" in §5 is stated too firmly.
  - It is also unknown whether the decline continues after 24 months. "Not disappeared" applies only to 24 months.
- **The control offices' meeting audit is contamination.** It happened in month 15, plausibly prompted by the published nine-month findings.
  - It narrows the treated–control contrast, so it biases the estimate toward zero. Report a sensitivity analysis excluding those two offices.
  - Their own +4.1% is a before–after comparison in two offices, open to regression to the mean and seasonality. The hedging in the text is appropriate.
- **"Upper bound" for the Halden continuers is too strong.** With no comparison group, background trends could push their figures in either direction. "Likely favourable to reduced hours" is safer.
  - Response is also 14 of 23, from an already non-random 23.
- **Early termination of the counter arm should be reported as a deviation from protocol.** Also, if staff costs are part rather than all of cost per contact, 12% more staff giving about 9% higher cost per contact makes sense. Say that this is the assumption.
- **No intervals for sick days and resignations.** Neither outcome has an interval, at either time point.
- **The rebuttal of the re-analysis's novelty argument is fair but cross-population.** The month-ten extrapolation came from Halden volunteers. Varden staff were randomised rather than self-selected, which arguably makes a novelty effect less likely there, not more. The report could make that point explicitly.
- **Authorship.** R. Okafor is a co-author of the original Halden pilot. It would be good to note that the original "sector-general" conclusion is now revised, since the reverters and the counter-arm termination bear directly on it.

## 4. Where the series now stands

| Question | State of evidence |
|---|---|
| Per-hour gain in discretionary work | Real, about 8–10% at 24 months in one randomised trial; consistent with the meta-analysis's corrected range |
| Persistence | Partial decline (about a fifth, like-for-like) from 9 to 24 months; not established statistically; beyond 24 months unknown |
| Mechanism | Meeting reduction supported by a registered re-test on the same offices; accounting suggests it may explain most of the gain; independent replication needed |
| Coverage-bound work | Clear per-employee loss; restoring service costs about 9–12% more; the county ended that arm |
| Gains without cutting hours | Suggestive but uncontrolled (two control offices); the key untested design is an arm that reorganises without cutting hours |

The authors' closing point identifies the most useful next trial. If cutting meetings delivers most of the gain, the policy question shifts from whether to cut hours to whether a shorter week is needed to make reorganisation happen and stick. Only a trial with a reorganise-only arm can answer that.

I can draft a corrected Summary paragraph or a short note on the log-hours measure if helpful.
